answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1882–1956 · English essayist, playwright and creator of Winnie-the-Pooh
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and pinned to the page. The sentence closes a paragraph on page 90 of Milne’s essay “The Record Lie,” in his 1920 collection If I May (Methuen & Co., London) — confirmed in the scanned first edition and in the full text at Project Gutenberg. Milne’s own opening word is For, which the popular version drops.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Page 90, confirmed in the scanned first edition

source.excerpt: Two thousand years from now people will still be quoting it, and killing each other on the strength of it. Or perhaps I am wrong. Perhaps two thousand years from now, if the English language is sufficiently dead by then, the world will have some casual paradox of Bernard Shaw’s or Oscar Wilde’s on its lips, passing it reverently from mouth to mouth as if it were Holy Writ, and dropping bombs on Mars to show that they know what it means. For a quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that Milne should receive credit for the remark, citing the essay “The Record Lie” in the 1920 collection, start page 89, quote page 90, Methuen & Company, London.

We opened the same edition. The Internet Archive scan of the London Methuen 1920 printing ↗ carries the sentence on page 90, exactly as cited, closing the paragraph about Bernard Shaw and Oscar Wilde.
Project Gutenberg’s full text of If I May ↗ reproduces the same passage, so the wording can be checked without the scan.

Wikiquote’s Milne page ↗ does not list this line at all — its quote sections cover only the four Pooh and children’s-verse books, which is a fair measure of how thoroughly the adult essays have been eclipsed.
source.excerptNote: Note Milne’s opening word: For. The famous version begins “A quotation…”, which severs the sentence from the paragraph it was written to explain.

source.useLine: Free to use in the US, including in commercial and paid presentations — no permission or licence needed. Outside the US it is not so simple: Milne died on 31 January 1956, so in life-plus-70 countries (UK/EU) the essay stays in copyright until 1 January 2027.
source.rightsNote: If I May was first published in 1920 by Methuen & Co. in London — comfortably before the 1931 cutoff for United States copyright — so the essay and this sentence are in the public domain in the US. author.name: A. A. Milne
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1882–1956 · English essayist, playwright and creator of Winnie-the-Pooh
author.bio: Alan Alexander Milne (18 January 1882 – 31 January 1956) joined the staff of Punch in 1906 and became its assistant editor, building a career as a humorist, playwright and novelist long before the bear arrived. He was commissioned into the Royal Warwickshire Regiment in 1915, served on the Somme from July to November 1916, and was invalided home with trench fever. The Pooh books of 1926 and 1928 came to overshadow everything else he wrote — which is why an adult essay line like this one is so often filed under the wrong shelf.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right — unusually, for a Milne quotation. What gets mangled is the wording, the setting and the citation.

items.why: Milne wrote “For a quotation is a handy thing to have about…” — the For chains the sentence to the argument it explains. Circulating versions cut it silently; Goodreads at least brackets the repair as “[A] quotation…” ↗, which is honest but still hides what the sentence was answering.

items.who: Filed as a whimsical thought about quoting
items.why: Aggregators print it bare — LibQuotes credits only If I May ↗, with no essay named. In the book it is the hinge of an attack on Si vis pacem, para bellum, two sentences after Milne pictures people still “killing each other on the strength of it” in two thousand years’ time.
AZQuotes sources it to “The Red House Mystery and Other Novels” (eBookIt.com, 2013), p. 1247 ↗ — a modern ebook compilation, not the 1920 essay collection where the sentence actually first appeared.

items.who: Dorothy L. Sayers / Lord Peter Wimsey
items.why: Quote Investigator records Sayers’ 1932 novel Have His Carcase ↗, where Wimsey says “I always have a quotation for everything—it saves original thinking.” A similar notion in different words; the two are sometimes blurred together.

misattribution.truthLine: Milne really wrote it, and you can read it in his own first edition: page 90 of If I May, Methuen, 1920 ↗.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: It sounds like a light remark about the habit of quoting. It is actually the sting in an anti-war essay. In “The Record Lie,” Milne — who had served on the Somme in 1916 and been invalided home with trench fever — opens by complaining that he has “just seen it quoted again”: Si vis pacem, para bellum, if you want peace, prepare for war. He calls it “the record lie of the ages, the lie which has caused more suffering than anything the Devil could have invented for himself,” and imagines the Roman who coined it as a fat, easy-going gentleman who threw off good things after dinner and admitted he did not quite know what it meant.

The line about quotations is the pivot. Milne has just predicted that people will still be repeating the tag two thousand years hence, “killing each other on the strength of it” — and then explains why: a ready-made phrase spares you the work of thinking. The target is not quotation as a pastime. It is the borrowed slogan doing the arguing.
detailsBody: Milne pressed the argument much further in Peace with Honour (1934), a denunciation of war, then walked it back in War with Honour (1940). During the Second World War he served as a captain in the British Home Guard at Hartfield and Forest Row. Quote Investigator notes the same reversal: the events of the war caused him to re-evaluate his pacifist position.

The sentence has kept working as Milne intended. Quote Investigator records a Louisville Courier-Journal columnist, Tim Sullivan, reprinting it on 28 September 2014 while debunking the same Latin adage — “an adage popular among defense contractors” — and noting that the celebrated author of Winnie the Pooh “once went all Eeyore on the subject of quotations.”
context.pull: Two thousand years from now people will still be quoting it, and killing each other on the strength of it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes A. A. Milne should receive credit for the remark, citing the essay "The Record Lie" in If I May, 1920, Methuen & Company, London, start page 89, quote page 90; and records Dorothy L. Sayers' 1932 Have His Carcase line "I always have a quotation for everything—it saves original thinking", plus a 28 September 2014 Louisville Courier-Journal column by Tim Sullivan reprinting Milne's remark. QI also notes Milne later re-evaluated his pacifism and joined the British Home Guard.

The scanned 1920 London Methuen first edition of If I May contains, on page 90 in the essay "The Record Lie" (which begins on page 89), the sentence "For a quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business." — preceded by the passage about Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde and dropping bombs on Mars, and by the phrase "the record lie of the ages, the lie which has caused more suffering than anything the Devil could have invented for himself". Item metadata: creator Milne, A. A. (Alan Alexander), 1882-1956; publisher London : Methuen; date 1920.

Project Gutenberg's full text of If I May contains the essay "The Record Lie" including the sentence "For a quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business." and the surrounding argument about Si vis pacem, para bellum.
Project Gutenberg lists If I May by Milne, A. A. (Alan Alexander), 1882-1956, eBook #7365, as public domain in the USA.

A. A. Milne (Alan Alexander Milne), 18 January 1882 – 31 January 1956, English novelist, playwright and poet; joined the staff of Punch in 1906 and became assistant editor; commissioned into the Royal Warwickshire Regiment in 1915, served on the Somme July–November 1916 and was invalided home with trench fever; wrote Peace with Honour (1934), retracted somewhat in War with Honour (1940); was a captain in the British Home Guard in Hartfield & Forest Row during WWII; If I May is listed among his works with the date 1920.
"Si vis pacem, para bellum" translates as "If you want peace, prepare for war" and is adapted from Vegetius' De Re Militari; the page does not mention A. A. Milne.

Goodreads displays the quote beginning with a bracketed "[A]" — "[A] quotation is a handy thing to have about, saving one the trouble of thinking for oneself, always a laborious business." — credited to A.A. Milne, source listed as If I May.
AZQuotes displays the quote credited to A. A. Milne and cites it to A. A. Milne (2013), "The Red House Mystery and Other Novels", p.1247, eBookIt.com — not the 1920 essay collection.
LibQuotes displays the quote credited to A. A. Milne with the source given only as If I May (1921 edition), naming no essay.

The Online Books Page listing for A. A. Milne includes If I May, Methuen, 1920 (page images at HathiTrust, US access only), alongside later editions including E. P. Dutton 1921, Methuen 1921, Dutton 1925, Dutton 1926 and Methuen 1930.

Wikiquote's A. A. Milne page does not contain this quotation; its quote sections cover only When We Were Very Young, Winnie-the-Pooh, Now We Are Six and The House at Pooh Corner, and it has no Misattributed or Disputed section.
